title: Facade (structural)
points: One simple class that hides a complicated subsystem of several classes behind a small, easy interface.
The client calls one method; the facade coordinates the subsystem objects in the right order.
It doesn't add new behaviour, it simplifies using what is already there.
trade: Reduces coupling: clients depend on one class instead of many (Law of Demeter, SoC) and the call order lives in one place (DRY). Risks: it can grow into a god class (SRP), and clients can still bypass it. A Spring service coordinating several services is often a facade. Decorator wraps one object with the same interface to add behaviour; Facade gives a new, simpler interface over many objects. Adapter converts one interface to the one a client expects.
test: A controller calls inventory, payment, shipping and email services in a fixed order in three different endpoints. What pattern fixes this, and which principles does it support? How is it different from Decorator?
answer: Facade: one OrderFacade owns the sequence. It supports DRY, SoC and Law of Demeter. Decorator wraps one object with the same interface to add behaviour; Facade offers a new simpler interface over many objects.

questions.question: Three endpoints each call inventory, payment, shipping and email services in the same order. Which pattern removes the repetition and the coupling?
questions.explanation: Facade: one class owns the sequence and gives clients a single simple call. It is a new interface over many objects, unlike Decorator, which wraps one object with the same interface.
